title: Control for autonomous driving
body: How a vehicle follows a plan and corrects mistakes
notes: Teach this as a concept-led lecture with instructor demonstrations. Allow approximately 65–80 minutes depending on discussion. Students do not need to calculate commands, derive formulas, complete worksheets, or export results. Use the visual behavior to explain what each controller responds to and where its assumptions matter.

title: What students should understand
body: How feedback helps a vehicle recover from a mistake.
How different controllers decide to accelerate or steer.
Why delay, physical limits, and a poor model can spoil a good plan.
notes: The goal is an explanation in ordinary language. Students should distinguish a target-point tracker from error feedback and predictive planning. Use questions about what they see. Avoid turning this into a gain-calculation or optimization-derivation lesson.

title: Planning chooses; control follows
body: Planning chooses a path and a desired speed.
Control keeps adjusting the vehicle toward that plan.
The road, the vehicle, and imperfect information affect the result.
notes: Connect to Lecture 7. A route or trajectory is an intention; steering and propulsion must carry it out. A plan can be reasonable while tracking is poor because the actuator is slow. A controller also cannot rescue every impossible plan. The speed and steering demonstrations isolate the two tasks.

title: Feedback: look, act, look again
body: Observe the vehicle|Where are we now?
Compare with the plan|What needs correcting?
Adjust the controls|Accelerate, brake, or steer
notes: Follow the loop aloud, then repeat it. Each command changes the situation, so the controller must keep observing. A disturbance such as a hill enters between decisions. The demo uses exact simulated position and speed; real vehicles depend on estimates that can be delayed or noisy.
caption: A correction changes the situation. The next measurement closes the loop.

title: Reacting and anticipating work together
body: Notice the slowdown and correct it
notes: Use cruise control on a hill. Feedback reacts to what happened. Feedforward anticipates a known load or bend using a model. They can be combined. The speed demo optionally compensates nominal drag; it does not sense upcoming hills. Keep that distinction clear.

title: A model is a useful simplification
notes: The teaching vehicle captures basic turning and actuator response. It omits tire slip, road friction changes and many real dynamics. Models make prediction possible, but accuracy is conditional. LQR and MPC use a local approximation, while the simulated vehicle follows the nonlinear turning model.
caption: A prediction helps choose an action; new measurements reveal what really happened.

title: What does good control look like?
notes: Read the traces qualitatively first. A path that looks close can still involve aggressive steering. Gentle commands can leave tracking error. The numerical details are available in the demo but are not a class calculation task. These observations do not establish real-vehicle safety.

title: How we will watch the demonstrations
body: Choose a named case and press Play.
Watch one feature: speed, target point, steering, or prediction.
Switch to a contrasting case and explain what changed.
notes: The instructor can operate every demonstration. Play shows time unfolding; Run 20 s jumps to the completed response; Step freezes attention on the next decision. No student calculations or submitted results are required. The lab saves a previous run for visual comparison. It works offline after extracting the package.

title: PID: three ways to correct speed
body: P reacts to how far speed is from the target.
I builds a correction for a persistent shortfall.
D damps rapid changes in measured speed.
notes: Explain the letters as present error, accumulated error, and change. The bars show which contribution is helping at the current moment; students do not add the bars by hand. Derivative action can amplify measurement noise, so the implementation filters it. This display is a sample from the hill scenario.

title: Watch: holding speed on a hill
body: With P alone, speed settles below the target.
Adding I builds the extra push that is missing.
Watch the gap close after the hill begins.
notes: Load P on a hill, press Play, and point out the persistent gap. Then load PI on a hill. The dashed saved speed trace allows a direct comparison. Both presets disable D so the contrast isolates the added integral term. Ask why correcting a persistent shortfall is useful; do not calculate the final speed.

title: When correction keeps building up
body: The actuator is already doing all it can.
The controller keeps remembering the shortfall.
That stored correction can delay recovery.
notes: Introduce integral windup as a mismatch between what is requested and what is possible. This braking case starts with acceleration toward a target and later lowers that target. The shown overshoot and recovery are computed by the demo with anti-windup off. Explain the memory effect without integral notation.

title: Anti-windup respects the actuator
body: Pause the buildup when it makes saturation worse.
Keep useful correction without storing as much excess.
notes: Show the same braking case with anti-windup enabled. Compare the shape and recovery with the preceding slide. Anti-windup does not create stronger brakes or instant response. The implementation conditionally pauses accumulation; there are other engineering implementations.

title: Four ideas for following a path
body: Align and move toward the path
notes: Use this as a map of the remaining lecture. All four repeatedly respond to the vehicle state. PID is shown separately for speed. The categories are useful teaching distinctions; production systems may combine them and include additional compensation.

title: Pure Pursuit: follow a point ahead
body: Pick a target farther along the path.
Move forward and pick the next target.
notes: The orange point is the target and the orange dashed line connects it to the rear axle. The close-up uses equal horizontal and vertical scales so the geometry is meaningful. The target moves as the car progresses. Keep attention on the point and turning response rather than a curvature formula.

title: Watch: near target or far target?
body: May cut corners or recover slowly
The same choice may work worse
notes: In Pure Pursuit switch between Short lookahead and Long lookahead. Show the target in close-up, then play the motion. Use the saved trace to compare. These are tendencies, not a promise that increasing lookahead always helps. No angle calculation is needed.

title: Stanley: align and move toward the path
body: Is the vehicle pointing along the path?
Is the front axle to one side of it?
notes: Point to the front axle and the magenta sideways-error segment. A car can be close to the path but pointed away, or aligned but displaced. Stanley responds to both. The classroom implementation uses the core geometric law and a shared simulated actuator; it does not reproduce the full original racing vehicle.

title: Watch: a strong correction can arrive late
body: A stronger response tries to remove the error quickly.
Delay means the vehicle has moved before it acts.
Repeated late corrections can create oscillation.
notes: Use Stanley: Gentle gain, Strong gain, then Strong gain plus delay. Keep the path and speed fixed. The plotted comparison contrasts strong gain with and without delay. Ask students to point out repeated crossings or persistent swings. Do not imply that every delayed configuration oscillates.

title: Using a model to choose a response
body: A model of response|What a correction will do
A preferred tradeoff|Close tracking or gentler steering
notes: Introduce model-based feedback through the tradeoff students have already seen. A model relates steering to future error. The designer chooses how much to prioritize tracking and input effort. LQR turns that choice into a reusable feedback rule for the modeled operating conditions.
caption: The model helps turn a design preference into a control rule.

title: LQR: balance tracking and steering effort
body: Use a model to choose the feedback response.
Decide how strongly to value accurate tracking.
Balance that against large steering corrections.
notes: Expand LQR once as Linear Quadratic Regulator. Explain that it chooses a feedback rule under a local linear model and a cost that penalizes error and input. The words are sufficient; no matrices, gain-vector example, or cost calculation are needed. The demo also anticipates path curvature with feedforward.

title: Watch: change the priority
body: A steering limit can prevent the designed response.
notes: Load Balanced weights, Tracking priority, and Steering penalty. Watch both the error and input traces. Then load Limited actuator. Larger input penalties discourage command magnitude; they do not directly guarantee comfort or smooth steering. LQR here is designed without the actuator limits and lag, so clipping changes its behavior.

title: Why look farther ahead?
body: A bend is coming while steering is still changing.
Waiting until the error appears can be too late.
Prediction lets the controller consider future choices now.
notes: Introduce MPC with a lane change and limited steering response. This motivates planning a sequence rather than reacting only to the present. Preview alone is not exclusive to MPC: Pure Pursuit also looks ahead. MPC specifically optimizes a sequence using a predictive model and stated limits.

title: MPC: plan, act once, update
body: Choose a sequence|Consider preferences and limits
Apply the first action|Start carrying out the plan
Measure and replan|Use the latest situation
notes: Walk around the loop verbally. Future actions are provisional. After the first action, a new measurement can reveal a disturbance or prediction error. The controller then optimizes again. No horizon arithmetic or optimization derivation is required.
caption: Future actions are a plan. The next measurement can change that plan.

title: The green path is a prediction
body: It shows where the current plan expects to go.
Longer preview considers more of the upcoming path.
It changes when the vehicle state changes.
notes: Open MPC and use Step, then Play. Point out the green prediction ahead of the car. It is recomputed from the current state, not recorded future ground truth. The displayed vehicle shows applied steering while the prediction is based on the planned sequence. Different colors and a dashed reference separate those roles.

title: Only the first planned action is used
body: The orange point marks the next steering request.
Measure again before trusting the rest.
notes: This steering-sequence plot visualizes the same current plan as the green path. The point of the plot is the first-action/replanning mechanism, not numerical reading or calculation. Ask why an unexpected disturbance should change the remaining plan.

title: A preference is different from a limit
body: Try harder to follow the path
Consider more of what is ahead
See farther into a lane change
notes: Contrast soft preferences with hard input bounds. LQR in this demo has preferences but its design omits hard actuator limits. MPC includes steering angle and rate bounds in the plan. Neither controller can make an unattainable path feasible just by increasing a priority.

title: Watch: short and long preview
body: Compare how far the green prediction reaches.
Watch when steering begins and how the path is followed.
Tighten the limits and see what changes.
notes: The figure compares short and long predictions starting from exactly the same vehicle state; it is not a pair of completed trajectories. Use MPC Short horizon and Long horizon on the same lane change. Then show the corresponding tight-limit cases. Use After 2 s if inspecting the numerical details to separate startup recovery from the lane change. Keep the lesson observational; no result table or export is required. A longer horizon need not win every measure.

title: Prediction and execution can disagree
body: The controller requests a steering action.
The actuator needs time to carry it out.
Delay or a biased response changes the actual motion.
notes: The plotted Long horizon plus delay case separates requested, limited and applied steering over the complete run. The model used for this MPC omits actuator lag, command delay and bias. Even a well-solved plan can be inaccurate when those effects matter. Use the Added delay preset if there is time; do not focus on solver residuals.

title: Why a predictive controller can struggle
body: Bound the work and use a fallback
The plan ignores a real limit
notes: Discuss real engineering failure mechanisms. This demo has input limits but no obstacles or road boundaries, so a successful trace is not collision avoidance. It uses a fixed-budget approximate solver. The lesson is to inspect assumptions and the complete control loop rather than treat MPC as automatically superior.

title: Compare under the same conditions
body: Each colored vehicle follows the same path.
All receive the same speed and actuator conditions.
Change one condition and watch the comparison change.
notes: Use Compare: Baseline, then Added delay. These are independent vehicles, not multiple commands on one car. The default tuning is illustrative, so this is not a universal ranking. Students can explain a visible response without calculating a score.

title: Read the shape of the response
body: A brief startup correction can settle down.
A small typical error can still hide a large miss.
notes: Use the error history as a visual explanation. The horizontal zero line represents being on the path. Large oscillations or isolated peaks mean different things. Numerical details remain optional; no root-mean-square calculation is needed. The metrics use the rear axle consistently across lateral controllers.

title: Choose for the situation
notes: This table gives conceptual starting points, not deployment recommendations. A real vehicle may combine several methods. Choose based on the operating conditions, the available model and the physical actuator. Retuning, slowing down, or changing the plan can matter more than changing the algorithm name.

title: Other ways to improve control
body: Can it learn the right change?
Learn a policy or a model
notes: Keep this a brief overview. These approaches are not implemented in the demo. Connect each to a problem already seen: speed changes, uncertain dynamics or unfamiliar scenarios. Their design and validation requirements deserve a separate lecture rather than additional equations here.

title: Control depends on the whole vehicle stack
body: A feasible path and speed request.
An actuator that responds as expected.
notes: Connect perception, localization, planning and control. The controller is only one part of the loop. Delayed estimates or miscalibrated actuation can spoil the response. The offline demo does not communicate with ROS or physical hardware; use it to illustrate these dependencies.

title: Explain the idea in your own words
body: Why can remembering a speed shortfall help—and sometimes hurt?
How does aiming farther ahead change steering behavior?
Why does MPC keep changing a plan it just made?
notes: Use these as optional verbal discussion prompts. There is no written exercise or numeric answer. Listen for persistent-error correction and windup, the target-distance tradeoff, and the need to incorporate fresh measurements. Students should refer to a behavior they saw in a demonstration.

title: Explore again after class
body: Replay the named cases and compare what you see.
Use the concept guide or open optional details when curious.
notes: The package includes slides, a static PDF, six interactive views and a concept guide. It requires no installation or network for the demos. References and technical model details are in the README and speaker notes. Optional exports and fine tuning remain available, but no calculations or submitted lab report are required.
